scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The pas de deux originated in the mid-18th century as a ballet entrée featuring couples performing identical steps, evolving through the Baroque and Romantic periods to symbolize romantic love.
By the 19th century, Marius Petipa established the grand pas de deux structure with entrée, adagio, two variations, and coda, elevating the male dancer's role and making it a ballet highlight.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The pas de deux is performed as a central highlight in classical ballets, symbolizing romantic partnership and emotional connection between the dancers.
It often marks a climactic moment within a ballet's narrative, showcasing the principal dancers' technical and expressive abilities.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The grand pas de deux begins with an entrée where dancers enter and acknowledge each other.
The adagio features slow, supported movements with the male dancer lifting and steadying the ballerina.
Then, each dancer performs a solo variation showcasing leaps and turns—the male first, then the female.
Watch for Supported Adagio, Pirouette Supported, Lift (Portée).

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for pas de deux is composed in classical ballet style, supporting the five-part structure with tempo shifts from slow adagio to fast coda.
Orchestral scores by composers like Tchaikovsky accompany famous pas de deux, emphasizing lyrical melodies and rhythmic clarity to match the dancers' movements.
Listen for the Orchestra with strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion.
The pulse is Typically 3/4 or 4/4 common time at about 70 beats a minute.
The music transitions from slow, lyrical melodies supporting graceful, sustained movements to fast, energetic passages highlighting technical virtuosity and dramatic flair.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Marius Petipa is the key historical figure who formalized the grand pas de deux structure in the 19th century.
Famous dancers like Mikhail Baryshnikov and Gregory Hines have performed notable pas de deux, including in film adaptations.

While the grand pas de deux structure is standard in classical ballet worldwide, contemporary choreographers have created duos for same-gender pairs and incorporated more acrobatic movements, expanding the form beyond its traditional romantic male-female pairing.
The pas de deux descends from 18th-century ballet entrées and evolved through Romantic ballet into the grand pas de deux codified by Petipa.
